units: a rehabilitation professional describes two opposite attitudes among the people she treats
the first attitude consists in locking the injured joint and no longer using it
the second attitude consists in wanting to stretch the muscle at the very first appointment
the specialist judges that neither of these two behaviors is good
the absence of movement ends up weakening the joint and stiffening the muscle attachments
an effort that is too violent prolongs the irritation of the tissue
a colleague points out that the same uncertainty appears with hand injuries
both practitioners recommend moderate and frequent movement, stopped in case of sharp pain
they recall that recovery is judged over several weeks and not over a single appointment
text: A physical therapist says that her patients walk through the door holding two opposite ideas about what healing should feel like. One group wants a sore ankle locked into a rigid brace and left alone until it settles down on its own. The other group asks for a deep stretch at the very first session, sure that soreness must be the sign of progress. Neither approach works, she tells them. A joint that stops moving grows weak, and the tendons harden around it. A joint pushed too hard keeps the inflammation burning. A colleague of hers adds that people who hurt a wrist get stuck on exactly the same question. What helps, both of them say, is small movement repeated often, and stopped the moment the pain turns sharp. They finish with the part patients skip past: recovery is measured in weeks, not in a single appointment.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: healers of the past relied on an oral inheritance for lack of reliable instruments
this know-how was limited to a small number of practices
plant drinks were used against fever and against throat irritation
fragrant ointments were spread on swollen areas
warm plasters were laid on at bedtime and removed on rising
the drawing of blood was both feared and demanded
the healer's speech weighed as much as his preparations
giving the illness a name already brought relief
science kept few of these treatments but drew from them a lesson about waiting and trust
text: Long before medicine had any instrument it could trust, healers leaned on a memory passed along by word of mouth, and that memory came down to a handful of practices. Boiled plants came first: a bitter drink for fever, a sweetened one to quiet a throat rubbed raw. Then came the ointments, spread thick over swollen skin, whose scent alone was enough to persuade the sufferer. Warm poultices had their place too, laid on at bedtime and lifted again at dawn. Drawing blood stood apart from the rest, feared one week and begged for the next. And the healer's voice weighed as much as anything he mixed: he gave the illness a name, and the naming eased it. Out of that tangled inheritance, research has kept few remedies, though it took from it a lasting lesson about waiting and about trust.

units: the medicine in shell form first travels down the tube leading to the stomach
muscle contractions carry it down
the acidity of the stomach dissolves the shell and frees its contents
the folded wall of the thin intestine takes up the active matter
the blood then carries the matter to the organ that transforms it
this transformation lowers the strength of the remedy
the remaining share attaches to precise targets in the tissue concerned
the action rises to a peak then decreases as elimination goes on
a liquid preparation acts sooner because its active matter is already in solution
text: A swallowed capsule has a long way to go before it does anything at all. It travels down the food pipe, pushed along by steady waves of muscle. Acid in the stomach eats through the shell and frees the powder packed inside it. The drug then reaches the small intestine, whose deeply folded wall offers an enormous surface for taking it up. From there it crosses into the blood, which carries it along to the liver, and the liver breaks down part of the molecule, so that less of it stays active. Whatever survives moves out to the target tissue and locks onto specific receptors there. The effect builds, peaks, and then fades as the kidneys and the liver clear the drug away. A syrup follows much the same route, but it starts working sooner, since the drug in it has already been dissolved.

units: a string player sought advice for headaches that were cutting his playing sessions short
no disorder was found on the side of the eyes or the ears
the clinician spotted a clenching of the jaws during the difficult passages
this repeated clenching wore out the muscles between the skull and the neck
the strain spread toward the sides of the forehead and brought on the pain
the dread of the attacks increased the contraction and kept the trouble going
the clinician taught the player a short release between two pieces played
she added a deep breathing exercise to it
the headaches became rarer after one season
the player put his trouble down to the fear of failing rather than to his instrument
text: A string player sought advice about the headaches that were cutting his practice short. Nothing turned up in his eyes or in his ears. What the clinician did notice was the way he clenched his jaw whenever a hard passage came up. Held through session after session, that clenching wore out the muscles running from the base of the skull down into the neck, and the strain spread forward to the temples, where the ache began. Dread of the next attack only tightened him further, and the whole thing fed itself. So she taught him a short release to run through between pieces, along with a slow breathing drill. Within a season the headaches came less often. He decided in the end that his trouble grew less out of the instrument in his hands than out of fearing a failure in front of it.

units: an unpleasant mouth odor on waking rarely comes from the stomach
it is caused mainly by micro-organisms that multiply on the tongue and near the gums during sleep
the method offered holds five actions that call for no costly equipment
the teeth must be cleaned on waking and before sleeping, with the brush aimed toward the flesh of the gum
floss must pass between the teeth because the brush cannot reach those gaps
the tongue must be scraped gently to remove the pale film that settles on it
drinking water helps because a dry mouth sharpens the odor while saliva cleans
an appointment with the dental practitioner is needed if the trouble goes on
an inflamed gum or a damaged tooth can keep the trouble going without being visible
text: Bad breath in the morning worries a lot of people, though the stomach is almost never behind it. It comes mostly from the bacteria that build up overnight on the tongue and along the gum line. Five habits will handle it, and not one of them calls for costly gear. Brush when you get up and again before bed, angling the bristles toward the gum rather than scrubbing away at the enamel alone. Run floss between every tooth, since bristles cannot reach into those narrow gaps. Scrape the surface of the tongue gently, where a pale film settles overnight. Keep drinking water through the day: a dry mouth sharpens the smell, while saliva rinses it away. If the trouble holds on despite all this, see a dentist, because an inflamed gum or a damaged tooth can keep it going without ever showing.

units: two opposite opinions circulate in a neighborhood gym
one group defends sessions in a very hot cabin
these followers claim that their muscles loosen after sweating heavily
the other group prefers immersion in very cold water
the latter maintain that the pain switches off abruptly
the trainer of the place refuses to side with either camp
he explains that heat softens tissue and speeds up the flow of blood
he explains that cold numbs and calms the irritation of the tissue
according to him the two methods suit different moments
he judges that sleeping enough and drinking enough counts for more than these practices
text: At a neighborhood gym you can hear two camps arguing it out, and neither one of them gives an inch. The heat crowd books session after session in an overheated cabin, walks back out soaked through, and swears that their muscles have loosened right up. The cold crowd drops into an icy pool instead and claims the ache just switches off. The trainer of the place grins and refuses to hand either side the win. Heat softens tissue and gets the blood moving, he says, while cold numbs and settles the inflammation, so both of them are useful, though not at one and the same moment. What he really notices is that the regulars keep missing the plain part of it: sleeping enough and drinking enough. No cabin anywhere, he laughs, ever made up for short nights and for meals eaten standing up.

units: the care room sits on the floor above a food shop
it holds two rooms with little furniture
the waiting room holds only seats, a plant and worn magazines
the second room is used for consultations and holds a table covered in paper, a weighing device and an instrument for measuring pressure
the boxes of medicine are stored up high and sorted by ailment
the clean supplies are kept in a drawer, every injection instrument in a sealed wrapper
the tap of the sink opens with the arm to limit the passing on of germs
the caregiver takes people without an appointment three half days a week
she treats wounds, changes dressings and listens to the fears of those who come
the place is very quiet, only the cold storage device makes any noise
text: The clinic sits above a grocery store and takes up two rooms, with nothing extra in either of them. The waiting room holds a row of chairs, one leafy plant, and a stack of dog-eared magazines. Next door is where people are examined: a narrow table covered in paper, an old scale, a pressure cuff hanging on the wall. Boxes of tablets line the top shelf, sorted by ailment. A drawer keeps the sterile supplies, every needle still sealed inside its packet. By the window stands a sink whose tap you work with your elbow, which keeps germs from traveling around. The nurse who runs the place takes walk-ins three afternoons a week, dressing wounds, changing bandages, listening to whatever frightens the people who come. It is very quiet in there, apart from the hum of the refrigerator.

units: night rest was first looked down on before being reconsidered
it was held at the start as a hollow gap that had to be cut short
active minds believed themselves bound to sleep less
a later phase prized long waking hours as a mark of courage
exhaustion was then displayed as a distinction
studies run at night then showed intense activity in the sleeping brain
this activity covers sorting, the fixing of memories and repair
of late people count their nights and worry about a result judged poor
the writer holds that this measured watching is a mistake
he maintains that rest calls for steadiness, darkness and a calm mind
text: Sleep spent a long time in disgrace before anyone thought to speak up for it, and the path it took is worth a look. It counted at first as an empty gap, a stretch of time torn out of living, which hardworking minds owed it to themselves to cut short. Then came the age of the guilty sleeper: staying up late proved your drive, and exhaustion was worn like a badge. Research opened the night laboratories after that, and what turned up there was a busy brain, sorting, fixing memories in place, repairing. Lately the swing has gone the other way. We count our nights, we score them, and we fret over a poor result. That strikes me as a mistake. Sleep asks for no heroics and no watching over. It asks for steadiness, for darkness, for a quiet mind. Wanting it badly is enough to drive it off.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of a workshop of healing plants had not meant to take up this work
a lasting allergic reaction, poorly calmed, pushed her to look into what plant drinks were made of
this interest led her to study plants and then to work in a place of analysis
she saw that the richness of plants changes with the nature of the ground and the moment of the picking
she therefore made a check of each batch compulsory before it dries
this rule slowed her rate of making
impatient buyers left her because of these delays
the sellers of medicine trust her and take the greater part of what she makes
she refuses to announce cures and recalls that a plant drink soothes without treating an infection
her coworkers put the long life of the business down to this restraint
text: The woman who runs the medicinal plant workshop had never planned on the work. A stubborn allergy that ordinary treatments barely touched pushed her to look into what was actually in the herbal drinks people kept recommending to her. That question carried her into botany, and from botany into an analysis lab. Since she could see that the strength of a plant shifts with the soil and with the timing of the picking, she made testing every batch compulsory before drying. The rule slowed her output and cost her the customers who were in a hurry. It also won over the pharmacists, who now buy the greater part of what she makes. She still refuses to promise cures: an infusion soothes, it does not clear an infection. That restraint, her staff will tell you, is why the workshop has lasted.

units: a prevention scheme meant for the staff of a company draws a divided appraisal
the opening analysis is judged accurate
stillness in front of a screen stiffens the neck and dulls the shoulders
it also brings on pain at the joint of the hand that remedies do not erase for long
the answer chosen is a sound signal that cuts off the work and suggests a short loosening exercise
the first reactions report less discomfort at the end of the week
the carrying out is criticized for its lack of flexibility
the signal goes off without regard for the attention under way
many employees switch the scheme off after a week
the writer suggests letting each person set their own break times and taking up a discreet visual reminder
text: The prevention program offered to the staff at this company deserves a divided verdict. Its starting point is sound enough: frozen postures in front of a screen stiffen the neck, leave the shoulders dull and heavy, and bring on the kind of wrist pain that no medicine clears away for long. The answer it proposes is an audible alert that breaks off the task and suggests a short loosening exercise. The idea appeals, and the early feedback reports less discomfort by the end of the week. Where the thing falls down is rigidity. The alert fires with no regard at all for what anyone happens to be concentrating on, and plenty of employees switch it off after a week. A fix looks within reach: let each person set their own break windows, then trade the sound for a quiet reminder on the screen.
